# Exclusive: Menopause care startup Midi is raising $60 million, just 4 months after its last funding round

By[Rebecca Torrence](https://www.businessinsider.com/author/rebecca-torrence)

In the midst of a funding winter for tech startups, the wait time between funding rounds is getting longer, [data shows](https://www.businessinsider.com/late-stage-startups-vc-lack-funding-forced-shut-down-2023-10). That hasn't stopped Midi, an early-stage women's healthcare startup, from raising a new bundle of capital only four months after it announced its last round.

Midi, which aims to expand care for women experiencing perimenopause and menopause through a combination of virtual visits, prescriptions, and personalized care plans, is in talks to raise a Series B round, according to three people familiar with the matter. The company is seeking to raise $60 million, two people said, which would put its post-money valuation in the range of $300 million and $310 million.

A spokesperson for Midi confirmed that the startup is currently fundraising, but said the round hasn't yet closed. Terms of the deal could change.

The raise follows a September announcement that Midi closed a [$25 million](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/midi-health-raises-25m-in-series-a-funding-led-by-gv-google-ventures-to-expand-access-to-expert-and-affordable-midlife-care-for-women-301940403.html) Series A from GV, formerly Google Ventures, Felicis, Semper Virens, Icon, 25M, and Operator Collective, among others. The startup has grabbed $37.5 million to date, according to Pitchbook.

The fast financing shows investor fervor for Midi. Founded by Joanna Strober, a repeat founder who sold a previous startup to WeightWatchers, and Sharon Meers, a longtime managing director at Goldman Sachs, Midi has become a star player in midlife care for women in two short years.

It operates a virtual clinic that seeks to improve access to care for women as they age. Midi has leaned into a multi-channel distribution strategy, working with employers to offer its services as an employee benefit and partnering with healthcare systems to extend its reach. In October, Midi [announced](https://memorialhermann.org/about-us/newsroom/press-releases/midi-health-collaborate-expand-access-expert-midlife-care-women) a partnership with Houston-based Memorial Hermann Health System to offer telehealth services for menopause symptoms alongside care that the health system's physicians provide in person.

The company is growing quickly. According to one source with knowledge of the fundraise, Midi quadrupled its revenue year-over-year to $7 million in 2023. It's projected to reach $28 million in revenue this year, and aims to hit $100 million by 2026, the person said. A Midi spokesperson would not comment on the figures.

The company is seeing tailwinds as the conversation around menopause [comes into the open](https://www.businessinsider.com/vaginal-atrophy-from-early-menopause-at-age-37-2023-1), one source said. Michelle Obama spoke to People magazine about taking hormone replacement therapy, and [Drew Barrymore](https://www.businessinsider.com/drew-barrymore-first-hot-flash-with-jennifer-aniston-adam-sandler-2023-3) had her first hot flash during an interview on her talk show. McKinsey entered the discussion in January with a 42-page [report](https://www.mckinsey.com/mhi/our-insights/closing-the-womens-health-gap-a-1-trillion-dollar-opportunity-to-improve-lives-and-economies) on the $1 trillion opportunity in women's health. At the White House, Jill Biden is leading a new initiative to boost federal government research into women's health.

"Every woman, half of the population, will be affected by menopause," [Biden said](https://fortune.com/well/2023/11/13/jill-biden-white-house-womens-health-research-initiative/) during a press conference ahead of the announcement in November. "And yet, there's a stunning lack of information about how to manage and treat its symptoms, which can be debilitating."

Corporate America is also paying attention. Most menopause care startups, including Midi, sell into enterprises to offer the service as a benefit to employees. While only a fraction of employers offer menopause benefits today, more companies are [considering adding them](https://www.hr-brew.com/stories/2023/08/21/why-more-employers-are-investing-in-menopause-benefits) to attract and keep talent, and potentially save money. US companies lose about $1.8 billion each year from workdays missed due to menopause symptoms, according to a [Mayo Clinic estimate](https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/pb-assets/Health%20Advance/journals/jmcp/JMCP4097_proof.pdf).

Startups are one of the beneficiaries of this tide of interest. While venture funding to women's health startups fell in 2023, [according to CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/menopause-care-funding/), startups tackling menopause symptoms surged ahead of the pack. Data shows these startups raised $230 million last year, making up a third of all funding to women's health startups.

Still, the market is nascent. Midi's closest competitor is Evernow, which raised a [$28.5 million](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/evernow-raises-28-5m-in-series-a-funding-to-redefine-menopause-treatment-301518212.html) Series A last April. Like Evernow, all of the startups building exclusively in menopause care are [early-stage companies](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/menopause-care-funding/).
